title: The Sound of Your Voice
author: Krista Stevens
content:
What defines success when it comes to music? For Hrishikesh Hirway, who wrote four albums under the name The One AM Radio, it meant commercial attention. His interest in making music cooled after sales and airplay failed to materialize; he went 15 years without releasing an album. In this essay for The Bitter Southerner, Hirway looks at how he overcame perfectionism to write and record In the Last Hour of Light, an album heavy on collaboration.

“But Phil was echoing something I’d heard in the interviews I’d conducted and read about in books on writing: separate your creative, generative side from your editing, critical side. They push in opposite directions, and as soon as you start to edit, you’re no longer as free to play.”

“It was two days after my 47th birthday, which had left me feeling melancholy about reaching middle age and still feeling so far from my goals. I sat on my couch, put my headphones on, and played the album. Something had shifted for me. Somewhere around the third song, I felt something for the first time: I loved what I was hearing.

The music brought back memories with perfect clarity: what it felt like to write each song, to record them, the long journey to transform a part of myself into this music. It was no longer a question of the music’s worth. I can say to myself: this album is a document. And in it —listen!—you’re alive.”

title: A Mississippi Death Penalty Jury Was Seated. With One Black Juror.
author: Seyward Darby
content:
Earlier this year, the US Supreme Court heard an appeal from death row inmate Terry Pitchford, who was denied relief by the Mississippi Supreme Court after his attorneys claimed Black people were illegally struck from his jury. Investigative reporter Hannah McAlilly delves into the case, and into the wider problem of racial prejudice in the selection of juries in Mississippi:

A prosecutor struck a Black woman for having “red dyed hair” and in another, a prosecutor struck a Black man because he had “a ponytail, a sort of strange hair design.” That prosecutor told the judge he was concerned the juror might identify too closely with the defendant, who also was of a similar age. “Both have unusual hair styles,” the prosecutor said. 

Prosecutors struck Black jurors who, they said, seemed angry, irritated or inattentive. A Black woman was struck because the prosecutor didn’t like her “vibe.” Another, who worked a night shift before showing up to jury selection, was struck for being “fidgety” and looking “angry.” Another was struck because she “frowned a lot.”

title: “Days and Nights in the Forest” Emerges from the Shadows
author: @NewYorker
content:
Four city jerks, privileged and frustrated young men from Kolkata, head to the countryside for a few days of slothful rest and rowdy dissipation. They approach the locals arrogantly, seeing the region’s poverty as a source for cheap, subservient help and an open field for heedless riot, but a series of chance encounters—and romantic entanglements—sends them home shaken and humbled, though maybe not wiser. This is the premise of Satyajit Ray’s 1970 melodrama “Days and Nights in the Forest,” which had long been hard to see until the release, earlier this year, of a 4K restoration, which has now arrived on the Criterion Channel. (It will also be released by the Criterion Collection, on Blu-ray and DVD, on September 29th.) The film is a teeming, turbulent, confrontational meld of emotion and observation, placing the eruptive pressure of societal conflict amid the seeming trivia of social life.

“Days and Nights in the Forest” is based on an autobiographical novel by Sunil Gangopadhyay, published in 1968. The feature’s literary basis is underlined when two of the men reminisce about a literary journal they founded long ago, but it’s palpable throughout, in the freewheeling actions and impulsive dialogue, which Ray nonetheless films with analytical detachment and gimlet scrutiny—as befits a work of personal experience that, however, isn’t his own but the author’s. (Ray’s critical distance from the characters is as crucial to the movie’s emotional power as is his wide-ranging empathy.) The movie’s anecdotal aspect both abstracts and expands the drama. Ray’s incremental approach to the story elides through lines and plot mechanisms in such a way that the crisscrossing relationships and events form an intellectual map of the forces underlying them.

From the start, there’s something dubiously bookish—callow and potentially callous—about the four men’s rustic jaunt. As Ashim (Soumitra Chatterjee), who planned the excursion, drives, Sanjoy (Subhendu Chatterjee) reads to the others from the back seat about Palamu, the region where they’re headed. The book he’s reading from leeringly describes the locale’s women as dark-skinned and scantily clad; the four men’s minds are on sex and love. They tease Hari (Samit Bhanja), also in the back seat, about a girlfriend leaving him; he pridefully asserts that he “dumped” her, but a flashback shows what really happened. Sanjoy is similarly teased about his relationship with his boss’s daughter, another source of resentment that shows up in a flashback. Meanwhile, the hyperactive, sardonic Shekhar (Rabi Ghosh), riding shotgun, is unemployed and claims to have no time for the “bourgeois” frivolity of romance.

The melodramatic force of Ray’s film is built into these spare but potent character sketches. Douglas Sirk, Hollywood’s supreme director of melodramas and a theoretician of the genre, spoke of his films’ dependence on the contrast between “immovable” characters and “split” ones. In “Days and Nights in the Forest,” Hari and Sanjoy, in the back seat, are the “split” characters, their flashbacks revealing the division between their present-tense façades and their bitterly remembered realities. Sitting up front, Ashim, who is coolly brazen, and the antic, unreflective Shekhar—the king and the jester—are the “immovable” ones, with unified identities that are nonetheless exposed and vulnerable.

All four are manifestly bourgeois, flashing their cash from the moment they arrive at the village where they are to stay. They blusteringly order a bedraggled local man named Lakha to accompany and serve them. (“Ask if he can come with us,” Sanjoy says to Ashim in English, certain that Lakha won’t understand.) They arrive as self-aware screwups, who know full well that they should have reserved their bungalow in advance but instead hector and bribe the guesthouse’s beleaguered watchman into bending the rules and giving them one anyway. He fears he’ll be fired for it, and one of the travellers—again in English—quips, “Thank God for corruption.”

The men are keen to go slumming. At night, they go drinking at a shedlike bar where women, to their surprise, drink together as heavily as men do. One of the women, Duli (Simi Garewal), noticing the haughty and higher-class men sizing her and her friends up, boldly approaches them for drinking money. The next morning, when the men show up at the local market in search of breakfast, a group of women, including Duli, are there in search of day labor. The men hire three, including Duli, to do their chores. One woman is pressed into service as a punkah wallah, charged with pulling a rope that keeps a hinged ceiling fan flapping back and forth and keeping the men cool. As for Duli, she sweeps the bungalow’s floor with a whisk broom, Hari ogling her as she bends over.

But Hari’s friends have other pursuits in mind. Shekhar brazenly asks Lakha where they can find “middle-class women,” and the poor man obediently points the way. As the four men walk the designated road, they pass a badminton court, where they encounter two women of the local gentry: Rini (Sharmila Tagore), a young, unmarried woman of intellectual ambition and poetic refinement, and her sister-in-law, Jaya (Kaberi Bose), a still youthful widow who is desperately lonely and the mother of a lively young boy. Surprised to encounter urbane menfolk here, the women lead them in a whirl of home visits—Rini’s father, Sadashiv (Pahari Sanyal), is a landowner—and social outings. Gradually, the women’s strong and probing personalities lay bare the weaknesses and presumptions of the ostensibly suitable men in their midst.

The men and women are instantly on familiar terms, and the push and pull of formalities and witticisms creates an atmosphere of brightness and romantic energy, although the household is darkened by tragedy and muffled by isolation. Rini guides Ashim to a small aerie that’s her solitary retreat, with her English-language books and her Western records (including “Rubber Soul” and “Joan Baez in Concert”), but their romantic connection is shadowed by her keen awareness of his cavalier, solipsistic arrogance. Jaya, with little hope of romance, seeks a sexual encounter, in a powerfully ironic scene contrasting the purity of desire with the fretful inhibitions of conventional morality.

As the story unfolds, relationships between friends, transactions with locals and bureaucrats, episodes of love and lust, and moments of painful self-awareness produce a subjective panorama of unredressed inequality, squandered energy, stifling tradition, and a restive quest for liberation. Ray gives his four men a natural exuberance and supplies them with a varied, pugnaciously expansive range of action. Whether in straightforward mealtime banalities or chatter when bathing at an outdoor well, or in the raucous ribaldry of their drunken rambles, they bring high spirits and a hunger for experience, albeit on their own presumptuous terms. Ray approaches the action with a vigorous yet reflective and piercingly probing eye. Observing the four men at the bar, his camera tracks from face to face, pausing at each before passing on, making palpable both connections and disconnections—isolation amid the overheated tumult.

The movie’s romantic centerpiece is a party game that the two women teach the four men during a picnic. It’s a memory game, in which the group sits in a circle, one member says the name of a famous person, and the next one repeats that name and adds another, and so on; those who forget a name are out, until a winner remains. For many movie lovers seeing the film for the first time, the game will be startlingly familiar, as it was more recently played in Wes Anderson’s “Asteroid City,” by a group of scientifically precocious teen-agers. (For that matter, the setup of Ray’s film also prefigures that of Anderson’s “The Darjeeling Limited.”) For both Ray and Anderson—who was involved in the current restoration and is a long-standing admirer of Ray’s—the demanding game gives rise to high drama and keen suspense along with tender comedy and rapturous romanticism. Both directors make use of its patterned and repetitive format to embody emotional extremes in a precise and formalized array of visual imagination.

The trivial outcome of this friendly competition plays an outsized role in the relationship of Rini and Ashim—a psychological wrangle in which the discerning Rini has the upper hand and lets him know it. (Ray films their climactic confrontation in intense, dual closeups, framed starkly against the sky, that are as indiscreetly intimate as they are sculpturally grand.) There’s another struggle, between Hari and Duli, that’s altogether more troubling, because of the inherent inequality of the relationship—between an educated middle-class man and a desperately poor and unworldly woman of doubtless little schooling who is also in his employ. Ray pays close attention to the fine points of the abusive relationship—including the confusion of emotion and the bedrock of money—and he situates it at the violent edge of class conflict and stifled revolt.

“Days and Nights in the Forest” came near the midpoint of Ray’s career. By 1970, he’d made more than a dozen features since his Neo Realist-inspired début, “Pather Panchali,” from 1955 (the first entry in his Apu trilogy, completed in 1959), and his work ranged from the historicist formalism of “The Music Room” to the ferocious urban feminism of “The Big City” to the time-shifting political modernism of “The Hero” to the antic musical fantasy of “The Adventures of Goopy and Bagha.” (He made his final dramatic feature in 1991, at the age of sixty-nine, the year before his death.) With “Days and Nights in the Forest,” he varies tones and moods widely within one drama as if also turning inward, considering urban intellectuals’ distance from India at large, the differences of experience, background, and identity that make connections either a struggle or an exploitation. His four city dwellers head home with more than just wounds. They bear symbolic souvenirs, physical and verbal, that they, like viewers, ignore at their own moral risk. ♦

title: Astronomers Spot a Strange Atmospheric Wave Above Saturn’s South Pole - Nautilus
content:
Meteorologically speaking, every day is different on Earth—or every hour, depending on where in the world you live. That’s not the case on the gas giant Saturn, where storms and atmospheric waves can remain relatively stable across decades, or even centuries.

Featured Video

To take as one example: the fixed pattern of hexagonal winds above Saturn’s north pole. It’s been there for the last 40 years or so and was first spotted by the Voyager probes in 1980 and 1981. Now, though, the planet’s south pole has raised the stakes, with its own decagon-shaped (that is, 10-sided) wind pattern that appears to have formed between 2023 and 2025.

Initial images of the wave were captured by the Hubble Space Telescope in 2023, but further photos from Hubble and ground-based stations have provided us with a much better look, helped by the changing (and in this case, accommodating) tilt of Saturn. The results of the latest analysis were recently published in Science Advances.

Read more: “See Saturn Like You’ve Never Seen It Before”

The decagon wave is apparently created by a fast-moving eastward wind current and is moving at a rate of 8.2 feet per second, stretching down into many layers of Saturn’s turbulent atmosphere. It’s huge, too, with each side of the decagon measuring more than 55,000 miles. It’s so big, in fact, that you could fit Earth inside it three or four times over. It has a “wobble” to it as well, shifting its position on a 32-day cycle. This is an interesting comparison point with the north pole hexagon, which is much more fixed.

As for how it’s being formed, the study authors ran simulations of the decagon to try to understand the underlying mechanics. It’s possible that the well-known Red Spot storm on Saturn is having some influence, causing repeated disruption to winds that settles into a pattern. Another theory is that the planet’s rotation and the powerful jet streams that the decagon is flowing inside are creating a trap for atmospheric waves to travel along, creating the distinctive shape.

That said, these are all early observations, and there are still lots of questions to answer about Saturn’s latest feature. So for now, the next time you’re stuck inside of a storm, just be thankful it’s not going to last decades.

title: Deadly Livestock Virus Found Lurking in Ancient Texts - Nautilus
content:
There was a time, long ago, when we used to write things down on paper. Before that, in the Middle Ages, the few people who could write copied things down on animal skin. After these skins had been washed, stretched, and scraped, they proved to be remarkably resilient, lasting for centuries. Now a new study into medieval codices finds they recorded a lot more than beautifully illuminated words—they’re riddled with viruses, too.

Featured Video

A team of international researchers led by agricultural scientists from the University College Dublin extracted DNA from the animal-skin pages of a series of archaic manuscripts. The texts they surveyed came from across Europe and included notable works like the thousand-year-old York Gospels, which were used in prior DNA studies, and the Corpus Christi College Cambridge, one of the earliest surviving English dictionaries. 

Read more: “Medieval Medical Misinformation Persists”

But it wasn’t the words they were interested in. In some of these codices, they found multiple pages containing genetic material from the sheeppox virus (likely because an infected animal made the ultimate sacrifice for medieval literacy). By examining the viral sequences from different manuscripts throughout time, the team was able to reconstruct its past. For example, in addition to sheep skin, some goat and calf skins were also infected with sheeppox, a sign of possible crossover infection events. To fill in the gaps bookending the study period, they compared the manuscript sequences to sheeppox virus DNA extracted from the teeth of Bronze Age sheep and modern viruses circulating today. 

The result was a comprehensive history of the sheeppox virus. The team discovered it diverged from the lineage of capripoxviruses (sheeppox virus, goatpox virus, and lumpy skin disease virus) somewhere around 11,500 and 3,700 years ago. It’s a time period that just happens to coincide with the rise of animal domestication in Europe. 

“We find that unlike the smallpox virus, the sheeppox virus genome was very stable over the last few millennia,” study author Louis L’Hôte explained in a statement. “This might mean that genetic changes before this point were very important to how the sheeppox virus evolved to infect its host, which may help us fight the pathogen in the future.”

You never know what you’re gonna find when you crack a book.

title: Philippines urged to drop charges against Indigenous protesters
content:
News

Philippines urged to drop charges against Indigenous protesters

Human Rights Watch urged Philippine authorities Thursday to drop charges against 11 Indigenous rights protesters arrested August 28 during a police operation to clear an anti-mining barricade in Kasibu, Nueva Vizcaya.

At the center of the dispute is North Luzon Mineral Resources Corp.’s (NLMRC) exploration permit and competing claims concerning land rights and consultation. The company said it consulted two communities twice in March 2024 and obtained certification from the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples stating that the permit area does not overlap with ancestral domain. Residents opposing the project say they hold a Certificate of Land Ownership Award confirming their rights as agrarian reform beneficiaries. They have petitioned the Department of Environment and Natural Resources to cancel the permit, alleging that affected communities were not adequately consulted.

Members of the Bugkalot/Ilangot and other Indigenous communities had maintained the barricade since May to oppose NLMRC’s mineral exploration activities.

Prosecutors charged the protesters with grave coercion under Article 286 and resistance and disobedience under Article 151 of the Revised Penal Code of the Philippines. The offenses carry potential prison terms of up to six months.

The arrests occurred amid longstanding tensions involving Indigenous communities, police and mining operations in Nueva Vizcaya. In 2020, the Commission on Human Rights of the Philippines reported that police violently dispersed an Indigenous community barricade in Didipio, injuring several people, and called for an investigation.

The 11 protesters were released on bail September 1, but the charges remain pending. Provincial and municipal officials have since negotiated a temporary agreement under which NLMRC personnel and equipment will remain outside the site while talks continue.

title: The Supreme Court Under Threat: Early Lessons in Judicial Self-Protection Harvard Law Review
author: @HarvLRev
content:
Because the Supreme Court is powerful, it is largely able to fulfill its legal responsibilities. Because it is a court — because it lacks both the sword and the purse — it is vulnerable to being defied successfully by Presidents and states and punished by Congress.

This Essay argues that the Court has become powerful despite being vulnerable because it has learned through hard experience to perform two roles reasonably well. The first is legal: The Court interprets and applies the Constitution and federal statutes in disputes before it. The second is political: The Court must survive in a world in which it ultimately must persuade powerful politicians to abide by its decisions. In short, the Court has two central tasks, especially when under threat — preserving the rule of law, and protecting itself. Commentators who believe that the Court should focus exclusively on its legal function fail to credit sufficiently the fact that, even today, the Court does not just act; it can also be acted upon — or ignored.

As this Essay shows, the Court began playing both roles early on. The Court made itself available to interpret and apply the law, as Article III of the Constitution and the Judiciary Act of 1789 directed. But the Court soon learned that it could not continue performing this legal function if it did not develop a way of practicing self-protective politics. Drawing upon several historical episodes, this Essay contends that the Supreme Court inevitably, and (within limits) properly, takes account of political threats to itself in exercising judicial review.

Part I identifies the reasons for the Court’s institutional vulnerability and the devices that the Court has developed over time to navigate difficult situations, including the current challenges facing the Court. Parts II through IV examine three episodes from the nineteenth century in which the Court successfully, although not always perfectly, navigated existential threats to its continued authority: cases arising out of the Jeffersonian backlash against the judiciary after the elections of 1800; Georgia’s defiance of the Court in the Cherokee Cases of the 1830s; and the Court’s decisions about military trials after the Civil War. The Conclusion defends the Court’s use of the tools of judicial self-protection despite the potential costs of such use.

title: What Happens When a Kid’s Robot Best Friend Dies?
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
In this story for MIT Technology Review, Sara Harrison explores the field of social robotics and the growing use of robot companions as therapy for autistic and other neurodivergent kids. These playful machines show promise: Research suggests that they can help children practice social skills and offer something overworked therapists and exhausted parents can’t—a patient companion, available 24/7. But Harrison also reports on their limitations and risks. Does this approach truly work? What about all the data gathered on the child? And what happens when a robot friend suddenly stops working and “dies”? A fascinating and unsettling look at tech that has moved into the most intimate corners of a family’s home.

While Moxie found herself in more and more people’s homes, Embodied still struggled to make money. In 2024, the company announced it would cease operations. Its robots—which depended on external servers that the company could no longer pay for—would descend into a deep slumber. 

Videos of bereft children who seemed to have become deeply attached to the blue bot began to circulate online. “I don’t want her to leave,” wailed one child in a TikTok video. Desperate parents posted on TikTok, Instagram, and Reddit looking for solutions. “My autistic child is devastated and I’m pissed,” wrote one parent. “Hope Embodied gives us a couple days to say goodbye,” wrote another.

title: I Went to the White House Brawl and Watched the Manosphere Go Limp
author: Brendan Fitzgerald
content:
I found it easy to resist the early dispatches from “UFC Freedom 250,” the Ultimate Fighting Championship event held in June on the White House South Lawn. But Jon Ronson is the sort of writer I can’t help following into battle. Fresh off a new book about masculinity, Ronson brings a delightfully skewed perspective to the fights and the days that surrounded them. The result is a portrait of a planned media spectacle that can’t quite make sense of itself. The best battle here may be Ronson’s tussle with his own photographer, 79-year-old Bruce Gilden, who is a bit of a hugger.

“I’m pretty certain you hugged Stephen Miller first,” I say. “I don’t see Stephen Miller as initiating a hug.”

“You may be right,” he says. “I don’t remember. Look, I do things maybe other people aren’t comfortable doing, but I felt comfortable and I trust my instincts.”

He acknowledges that “nobody is immune to misreading a situation” and that because of him we were all forced back indoors, but he blames Miller’s entourage for not checking with their boss on whether he minded being hugged.

title: How an Op-Ed in Support of Football Divided Oberlin’s Campus
author: @NewYorker
content:
Short on writers and needing to fill pages last October, Ava Harvey did what any sports editor for a small newspaper would have done: she assigned herself a football story. But since Harvey, then a senior at Oberlin College, was writing for the Oberlin Review, covering football was a rather tricky proposition. Oberlin’s team, the Yeomen, had finished 1–9 each of the previous two seasons. When Harvey began working on her column, during the 2025 season, the team was already 0–4, almost halfway to its eventual record of 0–10. A story breaking down Oberlin’s next opponent seemed useless. A feature on the team’s defense wouldn’t work, either. In its season opener, a home game against Calvin University, Oberlin had allowed its opponent to score seventy-four points before the start of the fourth quarter.

The Review has a history of publishing big feelings about football, keeping with the Oberlin tradition of having big feelings about a lot of things. Harvey decided that she wanted to write something “a little more controversial.” Her take? The school and its students should support the team more.

Had she stopped there, with a spirited call to fill the bleachers at Dick Bailey Field, that would likely have been that. But Harvey did not stop there. She felt bad for her friends on the team, not just because of their dreadful record but because of what she saw as a stark divide between football players and the rest of the student body. In her article, “Put Your Mouth Where Your Money Is: Back Oberlin Football,” she argued that “the majority of students are, at best, indifferent—if not outright hostile—to the sport.” She also noted that “the homogenized coastal culture historically propagated by the school”—despite Oberlin’s campus being in northern Ohio—“alienates Midwest athletes seeking a sense of home.” (Harvey herself is from Lansing, Michigan, and is a diehard Lions fan.) She pointed out that, in recent years, Oberlin’s best offensive season came after its newest recruits were prevented from visiting campus owing to the coronavirus pandemic. This was no coincidence, she contended: “Why would players choose a school where they’re viewed, at best, as an oddity, and at worst, as fundamentally incompatible with the institution’s values?”

After the article ran, something weird happened: people at Oberlin began talking about the football team. Friends told her that in the dining hall, where copies of the Review are often scattered like birdseed, some students were trashing the column. Harvey even noticed a spike in views of her LinkedIn page. About a month later, the Review’s opinions page published two responses, each taking aim at her rationale. The first called Harvey’s perspective “audacious,” adding that “the real issue with the piece is that there is no issue.” The second referred to the “illogical nature of the cultural argument” Harvey had made. Harvey felt like persona non grata, the lady who wrote that football column. “It definitely provoked a response,” she said. “So I guess I got what I was looking for.”

Oberlin is a Division III school that, by N.C.A.A. rule, doesn’t offer athletic scholarships. But having a football team, even one that never wins, is a suck on resources. As the Yeomen continued losing games last year, the larger college-football machine kept humming at campuses across the country. Ohio State, fresh off winning a national title with a twenty-million-dollar payroll, kept on buying separation from most of its peers. Down South, L.S.U. fired a coach to whom it still owed more than fifty million dollars, and then the Louisiana governor joked—maybe?—about having President Donald Trump choose the next hire. A core American truth is that football is a reflection of wherever it exists. Oberlin, it turned out, is no different, no matter how much it might want to be.

The most obvious fragmentation at Oberlin, a school of three thousand or so students, is right there in the institution’s full name: Oberlin College and Conservatory. There’s the liberal-arts college, and then there’s the renowned music conservatory. But just as at any school, the students are then split into many more subcultures, starting with those in the co-ops—student-run living and dining communities that essentially stand in for Greek life. There are also the journalists, the athletes, and the kids who spend sunny days doing contact improv, which was invented at Oberlin, tangling their limbs in the grass outside the library. There’s the Luddite Club, which last fall used a seventy-year-old typewriter to make a poster denouncing the school’s decision to offer students ChatGPT and Google Gemini subscriptions. There’s even a Let’s Talk About Death Club, which, according to its founder, the senior Bee Herbstman, holds “a lot of meetings that are about . . . death.”

Students describe Oberlin as a kind of oasis, a place where high-school misfits can find a community of outsiders. They also know that Oberlin is an avatar for the über-progressive, mad-about-every-micro-aggression school, which makes it hard not to frame their experience in relation to public perception. “It’s totally portrayed as Fox News’ worst nightmare, and maybe it is,” Herbstman told me. “But it doesn’t feel like the only thing we talk about at Oberlin is gender or feminism.”

“It’s like if ‘Portlandia’ was turned down a few notches and everyone was twenty,” Viv Tullis, a senior history major, told me. And so, when it comes to athletes, the traditional social hierarchy is completely inverted, especially as compared with other, more sports-centric schools. Tullis recalled that, back at her high school in Boulder, Colorado, it felt like “athletes were in charge of everything and running the show.” At Oberlin, she said, “it feels like it’s totally the reverse. I guess that does raise certain questions of what it means to be totally socially inclusive.”

To explain Oberlin’s social scene, Tullis used the dance department’s biannual show, saying that it might include watching spoken word about a performer’s menstrual cycle, maybe while the performer rolls around the stage. Or, she said, “it’s Friday night, you’re, like, let’s go crazy, and then there’s just a guy with a bassoon in the corner.” Such jazz parties, I learned, are one of the few settings in which football players and non-athletes regularly mix outside Oberlin’s classrooms. If the football team has live jazz at a postgame party, Lucy Wadman, another senior, said that she will try to get there early to snag a good spot where she can hear the music clearly. She does not, however, attend the football games themselves, at least not since the home opener her freshman year.

Oberlin won that day, one of two victories while Wadman has been on campus. That night, the jazz party, she told me, was probably the biggest party of her first three years. “It was insane,” she said. “Nobody cared, obviously, but it was just something to celebrate.” It makes you wonder what the Review coverage would read like if the Yeomen would just win another game.

Oberlin is not without some real football history. The last team in Ohio to beat Ohio State? That would be Oberlin, a 7–6 win in 1921. The first coaching job for John Heisman, of college-football-trophy fame, in 1892? That would be Oberlin again. And the school Peyton Manning almost chose before committing to Tennessee, when every program in the country was fighting for him? O.K., that one wasn’t Oberlin, but you get the point.

Football at Oberlin has not always felt so oxymoronic. But the true tradition, no matter the era, is the debate about how—or whether—football fits into Oberlin’s culture. “It’s part of Oberlin folklore to think of athletics as a problem, in some way,” Sebastiaan Faber, a professor of Hispanic studies, told me. Faber has been at Oberlin since 1999 and is in his first semester advising the student paper. “I think if you would run through the archives of the Oberlin Review,” he said, “you would see on the op-ed page regularly the same kinds of pieces about how football should be abolished, then people saying, ‘No, no, the football players that I know are also really good musicians and they love to read novels.’ It’s a permanent battle.”

When Khalid McCalla, a member of the Oberlin class of 2021, was looking to play college football, Division I coaches told him that he was too slow for a running back and too small to play linebacker. He ended up as a linebacker—at Oberlin. At his freshman orientation, in 2017, someone told him that there were three distinct groups on campus: athletes, NARPs (non-athletic regular people), and Obies. Ask fifteen Obies to define the term and you might get fifteen different responses. One clean answer is anyone in a co-op. But, broadly, an Obie is more likely than the average student to say “sportsball” or “athletic-type person” to describe an athlete. They’re also more likely to walk around barefoot, or to participate in activities like jello wrestling, as many students did during a weekend music festival last spring.

McCalla wanted to bridge these social divides, which eventually led him to quit football to do more on campus. (He was unhappy with how little playing time he was getting, too.) Another Oberlin graduate told me that McCalla was like a translator between athletes and non-athletes. But McCalla felt that some friends looked at him sideways for being on the team in the first place, because they felt that sports were “tools of the patriarchy or tools of oppression,” he said.

Still, the biggest challenges are on the field, all to play for a team that attracts few fans and very little interest beyond fellow-athletes. During a game, each side has eleven players on the field at a time, but a team’s full roster is much larger: many Division I programs carry the maximum hundred and five members. Smaller schools typically have smaller rosters; Hiram College, Oberlin’s first opponent this season, has a roster of sixty-eight. This year’s Oberlin squad, meanwhile, has just forty-one players in total. To compensate for its small size, Oberlin has seventeen players listed on the college’s athletics site with multiple positions. At the team’s early-morning practices, many players flip between offense and defense to prepare for any situation, especially when there are even a few injuries. “It does become a safety issue at that point,” a former player who graduated recently said. “I think the school has the resources and the ability to focus on it if they wanted to. I definitely feel for those guys and the future players who are coming in.”

The recent grad floated slightly looser admissions standards for football as a possible solution. I can already see the Review editorial slamming that idea. Harvey’s column, she said, reflected complaints that she had heard from a number of players, which included similar frustrations about the lack of, well, players. But what she hammered most was how, in her view, Oberlin has failed to make football players feel welcome. She wanted to see if the reaction might reveal insecurities, a sort of trick play for the truth.

As for Oberlin’s athletic director and the football team’s head coach, both declined my interview requests through a school spokeswoman, who instead sent along a three-hundred-and-sixty-three-word statement (plus a list of recent highlights in men’s lacrosse, women’s softball, women’s tennis, and men’s tennis). The statement recognized the roster size and injuries as a challenge for football, mentioning that the team has access to a sports psychologist. “Oberlin has always been a place where students ask hard questions, challenge assumptions, and debate what our values mean in practice,” the statement read. “Athletics is no exception. We see the student discussion about football as part of that tradition.”

Ghulam Woolman’s parents like to tell a story about a hike that they took when he was six years old. The Woolmans were with family friends. At some point, the conversation turned to Tom Brady and the Patriots, and Woolman didn’t know who they were talking about. He asked them to explain, not realizing how absurd of a question that was for a kid growing up near Boston, Massachusetts, in the twenty-tens. “It was kind of like being a six-year-old Catholic and not knowing who the Pope was,” Woolman told me. “Like, how did I miss this?”

When it came time for college, Woolman wanted to go to a school in a big city. He instead wound up in a small town in Ohio, having been sold on Oberlin by a performance of “Dracula” he saw at the end of a campus visit. He started there last fall as a freshman. He planned to get involved in theatre, but he also wanted to write for the Review. When Harvey published her football column, Woolman read it, loathed it, and saw an opportunity. And then, like a seasoned writer, he waited a month before publishing a rebuttal. “Obviously, being a freshman, starting as a staff writer, wanting to go into the opinion side of things, part of me was maybe, like, Oh, you want to make a name for yourself,” he said. “I feel like responding to this would be like tapping into the campus Zeitgeist.”

In his column, “Oberlin Does Not Need to Change Culture for Football,” Woolman said that Harvey’s logic was “shamefully faulty.” But instead of calling to abolish the football team, he defended Oberlin as it is, framing football as just another campus activity, not particularly deserving of face paint and giant crowds. “There is widespread indifference to the sport, but football is not unique in this,” Woolman wrote. “The indifference to football is the same people feel to soccer, or field hockey, or someone’s DJ performance at The ’Sco, or my standup. People go to events if they have a personal connection or if they have a free night and their interest is piqued.”

Woolman, like Harvey, kept on swinging. He described Harvey’s column as a “broadside that mischaracterized campus life and failed to appreciate what makes our college special.” This was the tame version, too, after a friend read the first draft and told him to rein it in a bit. “I was, like, you know what? I probably really should,” Woolman said later. But if Harvey wanted to use football as a mirror for Oberlin’s flaws, then he wanted to smash it into a bunch of tiny pieces. “I think people in the newsroom were kind of excited,” Woolman said. “Like, ooh, it’s sort of like a family fight, a staff writer and an editor going at it.”

“Actually having the football team is the inclusive thing,” Woolman told me. “And we don’t need it to be good for it to be meaningful.” In a vacuum, this was an intuitive argument: the idea that, unlike most of higher education, Oberlin can field a team without bending to the country’s football obsession. And yet another core American truth is that being normal about football is just about impossible. Nationally, there is more spending and attention on the sport than ever. The Senate is in knots over a bill that would try to regulate college football’s billion-dollar economy. The N.F.L. is coming for the night before Thanksgiving, as if Sundays, Mondays, Thursdays, Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas, New Year’s Eve, and some Saturdays weren’t enough. But as Faber, the longtime Oberlin professor, put it to me, the school’s desired self-image is as a “special place with a special way of doing things.” Preaching indifference to football, however radical that is, played straight into this sensibility. And so the column got “really, really big,” Woolman said, remaining in the Review’s trending-stories bar for two or three weeks. “Which, you know, you try not to get an ego about these things, but it’s pretty cool to see it up there,” he said.

After the Review ran the second editorial panning her, Harvey considered writing a response to the responses. But then the season ended, and then there were midterms, and then the semester came to a close, resetting the discourse until the next football column appears. It might even be here soon: the Yeomen, looking to win for the first time since November 26, 2024, have their season opener on Saturday. It’s a home game. ♦
